doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: What makes a singer a musician, and bandstand protocol
summary: Singers who know the language of the band, and respect for the bandstand.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I’m going to remember that one. That was a good one. As an aside, Rick Montalbano told me a singer — this is a joke but it really happened.

The girl wanted to sing a tune and he tried the key and she said, “that’s too high, can you do it in minor?” But it begs the question, what makes a singer a musician. And why does that question even exist? Why do some instrumentalists not think of singers as musicians? What causes that?

Well I think that there’s probably — certainly there are a lot of singers who are musicians. But there’s a whole lot of singers who aren’t. And what I mean by that is I mean I learned how to play the piano when I started to sing seriously. But I would never do a gig on the piano because I don’t play that well. But I could sit down and play the changes. I can hear the notes that are in the changes. I know what the bridge is as opposed to “the middle.” I’m going to come in at the middle or I’m going to come in anywhere. I mean I know the language. I don’t speak French but if I only spoke French and you spoke English we’d have a hell of a time communicating. So I want to speak their language. It makes them comfortable, it makes me comfortable. You know it’s more than the language, there’s a certain — I believe there’s a certain protocol up there on the bandstand. I mean I see things that are completely out of whack sometimes, that I see people do, that they shouldn’t do. Because it’s not protocol.
Can you give me an example?

I mean maybe I’m wrong but I mean, and I don’t want to be corny, but the bandstand is kind of a special place. So if there’s a trio up on the bandstand, or a riser, or even the floor, it doesn’t even have to be a bandstand, you’re not supposed to go up there and talk to them and hang out if you don’t belong there. You know there’s a certain je ne sais quoi that’s supposed to happen. And a lot of people don’t know about that. And maybe because today it’s a different world. Everything is okay. “Sure come on up.” But there’s a certain kind of a respect to have for each other and the music I think.
